title: One word, many meanings
subtitle: polysemy: fair, flat, capital, mean
summary: Work out which of a word's many meanings is intended - polysemy in fair, flat, capital, mean and other everyday words - and see how jokes play on it.

lesson.heading: Polysemy
lesson.text: A great many words in English have more than one meaning. Linguists call this aspect of vocabulary **polysemy**. Sometimes the meanings are clearly related: **flat** as in countryside connects with **flat** as in apartment, because both include the idea of being on one level. Sometimes there is no connection at all, and we call such words **homographs** - words with the same spelling but different meanings.

examples.text: The meaning of **fair** as in Book Fair has no obvious connection with any of its other meanings.
Words with the same spelling but unrelated meanings are **homographs**.

lesson.heading: fair
rows: It's only **fair** that we should share the housework.
adjective - proper, just, right
The Frankfurt Book **Fair** is a very important event for most publishers.
noun - a large show
The forecast is for the weather to stay **fair** for the next week.
adjective - pleasant, fine
I've got **fair** skin and burn easily in the sun.
adjective - light in colour
His marks in his final exams ranged from excellent to **fair**.
adjective - satisfactory, neither very good nor very bad

lesson.heading: flat
rows: The firefighters saved the children from the burning third-floor **flat**.
noun - apartment
The countryside round here is terribly **flat** and boring.
adjective - level
To join the Fitness Club, you pay a **flat** fee of 500 pounds.
adjective - fixed
The sonata is in B **flat** minor.
noun - a note a semitone lower than B itself
She finished the exercise in five minutes **flat**.
adverb - exactly; emphasises how quick the time was

lesson.heading: capital and mean
rows: Fill in the form in **capital** letters.
adjective - upper case
Wellington is the **capital** of New Zealand.
noun - the city where the government sits
You need plenty of **capital** to open a restaurant.
noun - money
**Capital** punishment has been abolished in many countries.
adjective - punishable by death
What does 'coagulate' **mean**?
verb - convey a meaning, express an idea
I didn't **mean** to hurt you.
verb - intend
He's far too **mean** to buy her flowers.
adjective - the opposite of generous, unwilling to spend money
The **mean** temperature for July is 25 degrees.
adjective - average
You shouldn't be so **mean** to your little sister.
adjective - unkind

lesson.heading: Why polysemy matters
lesson.text: Being aware of polysemy helps in several ways. The meaning you first learnt for a word may not be the one it has in a new context. Words can also change their part of speech: **flat** with its apartment meaning becomes an adjective in *a set of flat keys*. And learning a word's range of meanings gets you several meanings for the price of one.

examples.text: It also helps you understand jokes in English, as these are often based on **polysemous** words.

lesson.note: Context almost always makes the intended meaning clear.

lesson.heading: One word, four contexts: drill
rows: at the dentist's
an instrument a dentist uses to make holes in your teeth
in the army
training for marching
on a road-building site
a powerful tool used for making holes in a road
in a language class
an exercise practising grammar in a fairly mechanical way

lesson.heading: Jokes built on polysemy
lesson.text: English one-liners often turn on a word with two meanings. Recognising the second meaning is what makes the joke work.

examples.text: *I wondered why the tennis ball was getting bigger. Then it **hit** me!*
examples.note: hit me = I suddenly understood, and the ball struck my body

examples.text: *Smaller babies may be delivered by a stork but the heavier ones need a **crane**.*
examples.note: a crane is a large bird like a stork, and also a machine for lifting heavy objects

examples.text: *Time **flies** like an arrow. Fruit **flies** like a banana.*
examples.note: first flies is a verb and like a preposition; then flies is a noun (tiny insects) and like is a verb

examples.text: *You know prices are rising when you buy a winter jacket and even **down** is up.*
examples.note: down is soft feathers used to stuff jackets, and also the opposite of up in price

lesson.text: When a familiar word seems not to fit the sentence, assume polysemy: look for a second meaning rather than a mistake.

exercises.prompt: Match each meaning with the word that carries it in the lesson examples.

pairs.right: mean (I didn't mean to hurt you)

pairs.left: city with the seat of government

pairs.right: mean (too mean to buy her flowers)

exercises.prompt: In 'His marks in his final exams ranged from excellent to fair', what does fair mean?
options: neither very good nor very bad
exercises.explanation: Here fair is an adjective meaning satisfactory.

exercises.prompt: In 'To join the Fitness Club, you pay a flat fee of 500 pounds', what does flat mean?
exercises.explanation: A flat fee is a fixed fee, the same for everybody.

exercises.prompt: In 'You need plenty of capital to open a restaurant', capital means:
exercises.explanation: Capital as a noun can mean the money you need to start or run a business.

exercises.prompt: He struck a ___ and we slowly began to look around the dark cave. The teenage cooks were a ___ for any of the adults. Their marriage has been called a ___ made in heaven. Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: A match can be a small stick that makes fire, an equal in ability, or a marriage.

exercises.prompt: That bird has an unusually long ___. Keep the receipt when you pay your hotel ___. Parliament is discussing a ___ proposing changes to copyright law. Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: A bill is a bird's beak, an amount to pay, and a proposed law.

exercises.prompt: Hannah gave us a lovely ___ of glasses as a wedding present. Let's ___ a date for our meeting. My father has very ___ opinions about how people should behave. Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: A set of glasses, to set a date, and set opinions - fixed and unchanging.

exercises.prompt: I've applied for a ___ in our company's Paris office. The end of the race is marked by a ___ with a flag on it. Why not ___ your query on an online forum? Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: A post is a job, an upright piece of wood, and what you do when you put a message online.

exercises.prompt: The teacher hadn't had time to ___ my assignment. Sales have already passed the million ___. You've got a red ___ on your cheek. Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: To mark work, a mark meaning a level reached, and a mark as a spot or stain.

exercises.prompt: You need to be a special kind of person to ___ a successful business. Do you fancy going for a ___ this evening? Our shop has had a ___ on ice cream. Which one word fills all three gaps?
exercises.explanation: To run a business, go for a run, and a run on a product means sudden heavy demand.

money earned on an investment or paid for a loan

exercises.prompt: Which word - fair, flat or capital - carries each meaning?

items.text: a note a semitone lower than B
the money you need to start a business

exercises.prompt: In an army context, what does drill mean?
options: a tool for making holes in a road
exercises.explanation: Context decides: in the army a drill is marching training, at the dentist's it is an instrument, on a road it is a powerful tool, and in a language class it is a repetitive exercise.

exercises.statement: Homographs are words with the same spelling but different, unconnected meanings.
exercises.explanation: Correct - fair meaning just and fair meaning a large show are homographs.

exercises.statement: In the joke 'Then it hit me!', hit has only its physical meaning.
exercises.explanation: The joke works because hit me also means 'I suddenly understood'.

exercises.prompt: In the joke 'even down is up', what is the second meaning of down?
options: soft feathers used to stuff jackets
exercises.explanation: Down is the soft feathers used in pillows and winter jackets, so its price can go up.

exercises.prompt: Put this explanation of polysemy in order.
exercises.answer: A great many words in English have more than one meaning
exercises.explanation: This is what linguists call polysemy.
